wine.name: The Dead Arm Shiraz
wine.sites: Selected parcels of the house's old vines across McLaren Vale, many of them fifty to a hundred years old, on soils that run from sand over clay to limestone on the hilltops.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters and foot trodden about two thirds of the way through, the wine is pressed in a basket press and run to barrel to finish its fermentation. It matures for about eighteen to twenty two months by vintage, in new and used French oak in recent years, with American oak beside it in older ones, and is bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and liquorice over dark chocolate, leather and a savoury, sage like edge; full in body and dense, with firm, grippy tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Closed and powerful for its first five years or so, it then gains savoury, secondary notes and keeps well for two decades in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Shiraz glass.

label.means: The name of the vine disease, eutypa, that kills one arm of an old vine while the other bears less, more concentrated fruit.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the region south of Adelaide where every grape was grown.
The name of the house, taken from the family name of a mother of the family, with the red stripe across the label.

records.table: d'Arenberg's The Dead Arm is McLaren Vale Shiraz from old vines struck by the disease that names it, foot trodden and basket pressed. Dark, dense and chocolatey with firm grip, it wants years in bottle and a decanter.
records.story: The house dates from 1912, when its founder, a teetotal Adelaide racehorse owner, sold his horses to buy a vineyard property in the north of McLaren Vale, and his son made the first vintage there. The founder fell ill the next year and died in 1921, leaving the business to his son. His grandson, Francis d'Arenberg Osborn (1926 to 2022), known as d'Arry, left school in 1943 to help his ailing father, and took charge in 1957. He named the wine after his mother, Helena d'Arenberg, who had died shortly after his birth, and put a red stripe across the label, first used about 1959. The Dead Arm came in the early 1990s, from the next generation: by Decanter's account the name first appeared in 1993 on a blend of Cabernet and Shiraz, and the wine has been Shiraz alone from 1994. It is named for eutypa, the fungus that slowly turns one arm of a vine to dead wood while the other yields a little fruit of real concentration. In December 2017 the house opened the d'Arenberg Cube, a five storey building like a puzzle cube above the vineyards. For a sommelier The Dead Arm is the old way of McLaren Vale, the feet, the basket press and the barrel, in one bottle.

others.name: The Coppermine Road Cabernet Sauvignon

traps: Dead Arm names a vine disease, eutypa, and not a vineyard or a block.
McLaren Vale is its own Geographical Indication, closer to the sea and to Adelaide than the Barossa Valley.
The Dead Arm was not d'Arenberg's first wine: the house's red stripe label dates from the late 1950s, decades earlier.

report: The founder, Joseph Osborn in the library's holdings line, is described rather than named in the story: the house gives his death in 1921 aged 67, and no second source gave his birth year; his son Frank is described for the same reason.

The first vintage of The Dead Arm is not settled: Decanter has the name first in 1993 on a Cabernet Shiraz blend and Shiraz alone from 1994, a writer's timeline (not citable here, its address names him) has 1994; the record says the early 1990s and gives both years as Decanter's account.
The making rests on the house's sheets: 18 months in new and used French barriques for 2017 and 2010, 20 for 2006, 21 for 2004 and 22 for 2007, with American oak in some older sheets.
The red stripe label is 1959 in most accounts and 1959 or 1961 in one tribute, so the record says about 1959.

d'Arry's dates rest on the house, the Prince Alfred College page and an obituary summary (died 16 December 2022 aged 95); the library's holdings line names a living family member, which this record does not.
The library calls d'Arenberg the house most often named for McLaren Vale, a ranking this record does not repeat.

wine.name: RSW Shiraz
wine.sites: Old vines across McLaren Vale, the house's own and growers', one part from Blewitt Springs on sandy soil planted in 1969.
wine.making: Each vineyard parcel is fermented and matured on its own and blended late. The wine is aged in French oak, much of it of the Burgundian kind, for fifteen to nineteen months by vintage, with a share of new barrels, about a third to two fifths in the vintages read, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, dark plum and liquorice with vanilla from the oak, ripe and polished, with soft, supple tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release, it rewards ten to fifteen years in bottle in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large Shiraz glass.

label.means: The initials of Robert Strangways Wigley, the cricketer who built the original cellar in 1894.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the source of the Shiraz.
The house as it trades, at the ironstone cellars Wigley built and the Trott cousins rebuilt.

records.table: Wirra Wirra's RSW Shiraz carries the initials of the cricketer who built its first cellar in 1894. Drawn from old McLaren Vale vines and raised in French oak, it is ripe and polished, with blackberry, plum and liquorice.
records.story: Robert Strangways Wigley (1864 to 1926), a South Australian eccentric who played three first class cricket matches for his state, built the original ironstone cellar here in 1894, after moving to McLaren Vale, the house says, when he had embarrassed his family once too often. After his death the winery fell into ruin, and by the late 1960s only two walls and some slate fermenting tanks of the 1890s were left. At the end of that decade two cousins of a McLaren Vale farming family bought the land and rebuilt the ironstone cellars to their old form. The elder cousin, a self styled grape and chook farmer, gave the house its character: a bluestone tower, the Angelus bell above the cellars, rung to open and close each vintage, and a list of wines with stories behind their names. Church Block, by the house's account the first wine the cousins made under the Wirra Wirra label, came in 1972 and is the red blend a guest has most likely met. RSW Shiraz followed later, named with the founder's initials, as the house's Shiraz at the head of its range. For a sommelier it is a McLaren Vale Shiraz of polish rather than weight, and a way to tell a ruin's revival.

Church Block is a red blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz and Merlot; RSW is the Shiraz that heads the range.
Wirra Wirra was founded in 1894 but made no wine under its own label until the revival, with Church Block in 1972.

report: The revival year of 1969 is in a wiki and a winery summary, while the house's own pages say the late 1960s and the 1960s; the record says the end of that decade. The plan's why gives 1969.

Greg Trott, who led the revival, died in 2005 by one notice whose address names a living writer; no source gave his birth year, so both cousins are described, never named, and his death year is left out.
RSW's first vintage is 1992 in one source only, so the story says only that it followed Church Block; Wigley's link to the winery rests on the house, and his dates on two cricket records.

The oak months and the new share come from merchants' and reviewers' notes of 2009, 2010 and 2021 (16 months 40 per cent new, 19 months about 40 per cent new, 30 per cent new); recent fruit includes Blewitt Springs by the house.
The bluestone tower and the Angelus bell rest on the house's pages and a wiki; the bell's age and weight are left out.

records.place: Tintara, McLaren Vale, Fleurieu, South Australia

wine.name: Eileen Hardy Shiraz
wine.sites: Chosen parcels of old McLaren Vale Shiraz, the Upper Tintara vineyard planted in 1892 among them, with old vines at McLaren Flat in some years.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters in the house's open fermentation cellar, where its senior reds are made from February to May, and pressed in basket presses. The parcels are made and matured in small batches in oak barrels and blended late, the wine taking the Eileen Hardy name only where a parcel is chosen for it.
wine.glass: Blackberry and dark cherry with leather, liquorice and toasty oak, full in body and dense, with fine, ripe tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Tight on release, it opens after six to eight years and keeps for twenty and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour or more, an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large Shiraz glass.

records.table: Hardys' Eileen Hardy Shiraz is named for the widow who kept the family firm going after 1938. Old McLaren Vale vines, open fermenters and basket presses give a dense, dark Shiraz of blackberry and leather that wants years.
records.story: Thomas Hardy (1830 to 1912), born in Devon, reached South Australia in 1850 and worked for a year for John Reynell at Reynella before buying land on the River Torrens in 1853, where he made his first wine in 1857 at a property he named Bankside. In 1876, by the house's account, the Tintara Vineyard Company of McLaren Vale, founded in 1861 and by then bankrupt, came up for sale, and Hardy bought it; Tintara became the firm's home in the Vale. In 1938 the founder's descendant who headed the firm died in the Kyeema air crash, and his widow, Eileen Hardy (1893 to 1980), held the family company together for decades. To mark her eightieth birthday in 1973 her four children named the firm's chosen wine of the 1970 vintage after her, and the first Eileen Hardy Shiraz was released that year. The family firm merged with the Berri Renmano co-operative in 1992 to form BRL Hardy, and passed through larger companies after that, but the house kept its open fermenters and basket presses. For a sommelier the wine is McLaren Vale's link to the family that bought Tintara.

report: The plan's note is answered: the house's product page calls the 1970 the inaugural wine, and the house's history, Decanter and Wine Companion give 1973 as the release for her eightieth birthday; the record gives the 1970 vintage released in 1973.

The plan's why says the wine began as a blend across regions; no source read confirmed that or the Cabernet blends of the late 1970s, so the record says neither and gives McLaren Vale only for recent vintages.
The Tintara purchase is 1876 in the house's history and the South Australian History Hub, and about August 1877 in Wikipedia's Tintara article; the record keeps 1876 as the house's account.

Eileen Hardy's dates, 1893 to 1980, rest on the house's history (April 1980) and a Decanter sponsored page; her husband, Tom Mayfield Hardy, is described, his birth year being on one plaque only, and the record does not say how he was related to the founder.
The oak and the barrel months are left out: one merchant gives 18 months in small oak and nothing else confirmed them.
The Eileen Hardy Chardonnay's mid 1980s start rests on Decanter's thirty years piece of 2016; the integrator may wish to check it.

records.place: Amery, McLaren Vale, Fleurieu, South Australia

wine.name: Block 6 Shiraz
wine.sites: Block 6, a hillside of the Amery vineyard planted in 1892 with Shiraz rootlings raised from cuttings of Thomas Hardy's Tintara vineyard; about two thousand of the first vines remain.
wine.making: Fermented in the open fermenters the brothers built in the 1890s, some parcels plunged by hand and others under header boards, then basket pressed. The wine is matured in oak barrels for well over a year, eighteen months or more in the accounts read, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, mulberry and dark chocolate with liquorice and a saline edge, dense and powerful, with firm tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed for its first decade, it lives for twenty to thirty years in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Shiraz glass.

label.means: The single vineyard block at Amery planted in 1892, whose vines alone go into the wine.
The words recent labels add, for vines planted well over a century ago.
The name older labels carry, for the brothers and their vineyard at Amery.

records.table: Kay Brothers' Block 6 Shiraz comes from one hillside at Amery planted in 1892, fermented in open vats of the 1890s and basket pressed. Dense and savoury, with blackberry and a salty edge, it wants a decade and a decanter.
records.story: Two brothers of the Kay family bought the Amery property, first settled by an earlier colonist, in 1890, and the purchase was completed early in 1891, when one brother passed half of it to the other. Within a week, the story goes, they ordered sixty thousand cuttings from Thomas Hardy's Tintara vineyard, and in 1892 they planted Shiraz rootlings from that nursery into the hillside that became Block 6. Their first vintage, in 1895, gave a dry red meant for export to Britain. The open fermenters they built in the 1890s have stayed in use, beside a basket press. In the mid 1980s a member of the family first bottled the block as a single vineyard wine. About two thousand of the vines of 1892 survive, so the block is among the old Shiraz plantings of a region that has never seen phylloxera. For a sommelier, Block 6 is the clearest way to taste nineteenth century McLaren Vale vines, made much as they were.

The first single vineyard Block 6 is 1984 on the house's about page and 1985 on another of its pages, so the record says the mid 1980s; the family member who made it may be living and is not named.
The block was planted in 1892 by the house; one account says cuttings were collected in July 1891 and planting began on 18 July 1892, and another gives planting in 1891. The record keeps 1892.

The fermenters' year is 1895, 1896 or 1897 by account, so the record says the 1890s; the oak, new American with Baltic or Eastern European in the accounts read, is told only as oak, eighteen months or more.

The plan's note on the label name is answered: older labels read Kay Brothers Amery Vineyards, recent ones Kay Brothers Block 6 Old Vine McLaren Vale Shiraz. No change of ownership was found; the house describes itself as still in the founding family's hands, which the record does not state, as it may change.

records.place: Blewitt Springs, McLaren Vale, Fleurieu, South Australia

wine.name: High Sands Grenache
wine.sites: High Sands, Block 31 of the estate, bush vines planted in 1946 on deep sand at the vineyard's highest point, in the raised north eastern corner of McLaren Vale.
wine.making: Picked by hand from small yields and sorted, the fruit is destemmed to whole berries and fermented with wild yeast in open fermenters, with at least twenty one days on skins. It then matures on its lees for about eleven months in older French oak, in large foudres and puncheons, and in ceramic eggs in some vintages.
wine.glass: Raspberry, red cherry and pomegranate with rose petal, dried herbs and a fine, sandy grip; light on its feet for its warmth, with fresh acidity and long, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Fragrant and open within a few years of release, it keeps and gains savoury notes over ten to fifteen years.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant for half an hour if young; a Burgundy glass for its perfume.

label.means: The name of Block 31, the estate's highest vineyard, on deep sand.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the region of the estate.
The estate as it trades, certified organic and biodynamic since 2012.

records.table: Yangarra's High Sands Grenache comes from bush vines planted in 1946 on the deep sand of the estate's highest block. Wild fermented and raised in old oak and ceramic eggs, it is perfumed and fine, more raspberry and rose than power.
records.story: In 1946 a local grower and his teenage son planted the first Grenache bush vines on the high, sandy ground of the High Sands block, in the north eastern corner of McLaren Vale near Blewitt Springs. For decades the fruit went into other wines. At the turn of the century the Californian family company behind Kendall-Jackson bought the estate, its first vineyard in Australia, soon after launching its Yangarra Park wines. The first High Sands Grenache was made from the 2005 vintage, from the 1946 vines alone. In 2008 the estate began to farm organically and biodynamically, and it has been certified organic and biodynamic by Australian Certified Organic since 2012. The making moved with it: wild yeast, long time on skins, older large oak and, later, ceramic eggs, to keep the fruit's perfume rather than add weight. For a sommelier High Sands is the case for McLaren Vale's sand and old bush vine Grenache, and the wine to pour for a guest who thinks Australian Grenache is only sweet and heavy.

others.note: The estate's broader Grenache from its old bush vines, the wine a guest is likelier to meet.

others.name: Yangarra GSM
others.note: The estate's blend of Grenache, Shiraz and Mataro, the region's classic trio.

traps: High Sands is a single block, Block 31, of 1946 bush vines, not a blend of the estate's Grenache.
Grenache from McLaren Vale's deep sands is fragrant and fine, not the jammy style the grape is sometimes met in.
Yangarra is in McLaren Vale's raised north eastern corner, not in the Barossa or the Adelaide Hills.

report: The plan's note is answered in part: 1946 rests on the house and Wine Companion; the first vintage, 2005, on Wine Companion and Young Gun of Wine.

The Jackson purchase is 2000 in Decanter's Clarendon news and 2001 in another Decanter piece; Wine Spectator reported it as Kendall-Jackson's first Australian vineyard. The record says the turn of the century. One account names Normans Wines as the seller, not used.
The planter of 1946 and his son, the late viticulturist of the estate, are described: no source gave their dates.

The making rests on the house's sheets for 2017, 2019, 2020 and 2021: whole berries, wild yeast, at least 21 days on skins (2020), 11 months on lees in older French oak, with Austrian foudres and ceramic eggs in some years; 2017 was all older French oak.
The region record calls High Sands the reference for the modern style, a ranking this record does not repeat.

The respelling of Yangarra is the author's reading and rests on no source; the house is the Codex region record's, and the library does not hold it. The glass notes are the author's from the house's and reviewers' notes.
